chunks: "I'd give every one of them the same treatment. First I ask what it has to do and what it's allowed to cost: wall power or battery, how bright, how fast, how accurate, how big.
Then I draw sense, decide, act, plus power and communications, and put one real number on each block.
For variable LED brightness, I'd drive the LED with a low-side MOSFET from a PWM timer. Brightness follows average current, so duty cycle sets brightness.

I'd run the PWM at a few kilohertz or more to avoid flicker, and because the eye is roughly logarithmic I'd use a gamma table with 12-bit or better timer resolution so the dim end doesn't step visibly.
For brightness based on ambient light, I'd add a photodiode with a transimpedance amp into an ADC and close the loop in firmware.
The target is a light level on the surface, so the sensor must see the lit area and not the LED directly, and I'd use a slow integral controller so it doesn't hunt.
The security system, camera, tracking and eye-tracking glasses each get the same pattern. Security is mostly about low-power sensing, false-alarm rejection and a backup battery.
The camera is a bandwidth and memory problem: 1080p at 30 fps raw is already about 620 Mb/s.
The tracker is a battery problem: GNSS and cellular are the big spenders, so you duty-cycle them with the IMU deciding when to wake.
Eye tracking is a latency and eye-safety problem: infrared illumination, a fast small camera and a tight pipeline. Then I'd say how I'd test each against its spec."
